title: The Company
full_review:
Maverick filmmaker Robert Altman follows a behind-the-scenes season at the Joffrey Ballet of Chicago in the visually enticing but dramatically undernourished "The Company" (Sony Classics).
Dedicated dancers struggling to excel are the focus of the film, but the opening scene with a young man posing a lewd question followed by brief but gratuitous locker-room nudity rankles, especially as it is not characteristic of the film. In essence the movie is a valentine to ballet and those who strive to be part of that world, but the film is neither fish nor fowl; it lacks the force of drama and falters as a quasi-documentary.

To be sure, the dance sequences are lovely, some even mesmerizing. But after the first hour, with little developing in terms of plot and characterizations, it's a gradual downhill slide.

It's from a story by and starring former dancer Neve Campbell; she plays Ry, who is on the brink of breakout stardom with the ballet company. Juggling the maintenance of artistic standards with financial realities is Italian-accented Malcolm McDowell as dictatorial company director Alberto Antonelli. James Franco as a local chef provides the love interest, such as it is, for Ry.

Yet these lead characters fade into the backdrops as the only energy onscreen is in the beautifully rendered dance scenes, some set outdoors with weather adding an extra element to the dancers' efforts. The opening credits sequence set among colorful undulating ribbons is especially appealing and shot from assorted angles that add viewer interest. A rope dance is also a delight and the editing throughout, coupled with the crisp cinematography, should enthrall ballet fans.

In a meandering, unhurried pace, Altman chronicles the mundane details of the dancers' lives as they rehearse, sustain injuries, share cramped quarters and work part time, all the while committed to the ballet.

Romantic commitment is another story, however, as these young adults are seen as more interested in one-night stands than finding one true love. The view of young people working so hard to achieve artistic excellence may be inspiring, but not the implied message that casual sex is the norm and no big deal.
The nearly nonexistent story tells us nothing new about how dancers must give their all to their art, but for those untroubled by its narrative and moral lapses this tribute to the ballet offers artistic and visual involvement.

Because of a benign treatment of casual sex, brief nudity, sexual references and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
